title: Part 3, Chapter 5
paragraphs: Raskolnikov was already entering the room. He came in looking as though he could barely stop himself from bursting into laughter. Behind him Razumihin strode in, gangly and awkward, red as a peony, shamefaced, with an utterly crestfallen and ferocious expression. His face and whole figure really were comical at that moment, and fully justified Raskolnikov's laughter. Raskolnikov, without waiting for an introduction, bowed to Porfiry Petrovitch, who stood in the middle of the room looking at them inquiringly. He held out his hand and shook it, still apparently making desperate efforts to suppress his mirth and say a few words of introduction. But no sooner had he managed a serious expression and mumbled something than he glanced at Razumihin again and lost all control: his stifled laughter burst out all the more irresistibly the harder he tried to hold it back. Razumihin's extraordinary ferocity in response to this "spontaneous" amusement gave the whole scene an appearance of genuine fun and naturalness. Razumihin reinforced this impression as though on purpose.
"Fool! You fiend!" he roared, flailing his arm, which immediately struck a small round table with an empty tea glass on it. Everything went crashing to the floor.
"But why smash chairs, gentlemen? It's a loss to the state," Porfiry Petrovitch quoted cheerfully.

Raskolnikov was still laughing, his hand in Porfiry Petrovitch's, but was careful not to overdo it and waited for the right moment to stop naturally. Razumihin, completely thrown off by knocking over the table and breaking the glass, glared gloomily at the fragments, cursed, and turned sharply to the window where he stood with his back to the room, scowling fiercely and seeing nothing. Porfiry Petrovitch laughed, clearly ready to keep laughing, but was obviously waiting for an explanation. Zametov had been sitting in the corner but rose when the visitors entered and stood waiting with a smile, though he looked at the whole scene and particularly at Raskolnikov with surprise and what seemed like disbelief. Zametov's unexpected presence struck Raskolnikov unpleasantly.
"I need to think about that," he thought. "Excuse me, please," he began, feigning extreme embarrassment. "Raskolnikov."
"Not at all—delighted to meet you. And what a pleasant entrance! Won't he even say hello?" Porfiry Petrovitch nodded toward Razumihin.
"On my honour, I have no idea why he's so furious with me. I only told him on the way over that he looked like Romeo, and proved it. That was all, I think!"
"Pig!" Razumihin ejaculated without turning around.
"There must have been very serious grounds for it, if one little word makes him this angry," Porfiry laughed.

"Oh, you sharp lawyer! Damn you all!" Razumihin snapped, and suddenly, bursting out laughing himself, he walked up to Porfiry with a more cheerful expression as though nothing had happened. "Enough of that! We're all fools. Down to business. This is my friend, Rodion Romanovitch Raskolnikov. First, he's heard of you and wants to make your acquaintance; second, he has a small matter of business with you. Well! Zametov, what brought you here? Have you two met? Have you known each other long?"
"What does this mean?" Raskolnikov thought uneasily.
Zametov seemed somewhat taken aback, but not very.
"We met at your rooms yesterday," he said casually.
"Well, that saves me the trouble. All last week he was begging me to introduce him to you. You and Porfiry have sniffed each other out without my help. Where's your tobacco?"

Porfiry Petrovitch was wearing a dressing gown, very clean linen, and worn-down slippers. He was a man of about thirty-five, short, stout, even tending to corpulence, and clean-shaven. His hair was cut short and he had a large, round head, particularly prominent at the back. His soft, round, somewhat snub-nosed face had a sickly yellowish tinge but a vigorous and rather ironic expression. It might have looked good-natured except for the eyes, which shone with a watery, crafty light under almost white, blinking lashes. The expression of those eyes was strangely at odds with his somewhat womanish figure and gave it something far more serious than you'd guess at first sight.

As soon as Porfiry Petrovitch heard that his visitor had a small business matter, he invited him to sit at one end of the sofa while seating himself at the other, waiting for the explanation with that attentive and overly serious manner that is at once oppressive and embarrassing, especially for a stranger, especially when what you're discussing seems far too trivial for such solemnity. But Raskolnikov explained his business briefly and clearly, and was pleased enough with himself to even get a good look at Porfiry. Porfiry Petrovitch didn't take his eyes off him once. Razumihin, sitting across the table, listened eagerly and impatiently, looking from one to the other every moment with rather excessive interest.
"Fool," Raskolnikov cursed to himself.

"You need to file a statement with the police," Porfiry replied in a thoroughly businesslike tone, "declaring that having learned of this incident—that is, the murder—you wish to inform the investigating officer that such and such items belong to you and that you wish to redeem them. Or rather, they'll write it up for you."

"The problem is," Raskolnikov did his utmost to feign embarrassment, "at the moment I'm not exactly flush with cash, and even this small amount is beyond me. I only wanted, you see, to declare for now that the things are mine, and that when I have money—"

"That doesn't matter," Porfiry Petrovitch answered, receiving his explanation of his finances coolly. "But if you prefer, you can write directly to me, stating that having been informed of the matter and claiming such and such as your property, you request—"
"On ordinary paper?" Raskolnikov interrupted eagerly, again showing interest in the financial side.

"Oh, the most ordinary." And suddenly Porfiry Petrovitch looked at him with obvious irony, squinting and almost winking at him. But perhaps it was Raskolnikov's imagination, because it lasted only a moment. There was certainly something of the sort. Raskolnikov could have sworn he winked, though God knows why.
"He knows," flashed through his mind like lightning.

"Forgive me for troubling you about such trifles," he went on, slightly flustered. "The things are only worth five roubles, but I treasure them because of who gave them to me, and I must confess I was alarmed when I heard—"
"That's why you were so startled when I mentioned to Zossimov that Porfiry was looking for everyone with pledges!" Razumihin put in with obvious intent.
This was really unbearable. Raskolnikov couldn't help shooting him a look of sharp, vindictive anger, but immediately caught himself.

"You seem to be mocking me, brother," he said to Razumihin with well-feigned irritation. "I'm sure I seem absurdly anxious about such junk. But don't think me selfish or greedy—these two things may not be junk to me. I told you just now that the silver watch, though it's not worth a kopeck, is the only thing left from my father. You can laugh at me, but my mother is here," he turned suddenly to Porfiry, "and if she knew," he turned back hastily to Razumihin, carefully making his voice tremble, "that the watch was lost, she'd be in despair! You know how women are!"
"Not at all! I didn't mean that at all! Quite the contrary!" Razumihin shouted, distressed.
"Was that right? Was it natural? Did I overdo it?" Raskolnikov asked himself in a tremor. "Why did I say that about women?"
"Oh, so your mother is here?" Porfiry Petrovitch inquired.
"Yes."
"When did she arrive?"
"Last night."
Porfiry paused, as though reflecting.
"Your things wouldn't have been lost in any case," he said calmly and coolly. "I've been expecting you for some time."

And as if that were a matter of no importance, he carefully offered the ashtray to Razumihin, who was ruthlessly scattering cigarette ash on the carpet. Raskolnikov shuddered, but Porfiry didn't seem to be looking at him, apparently still preoccupied with Razumihin's cigarette.
"What? Expecting him? Did you know he had pledges there?" Razumihin cried.
Porfiry Petrovitch addressed Raskolnikov directly.
"Your things—the ring and the watch—were wrapped up together, and on the paper your name was written clearly in pencil, along with the date you left them."
"How observant you are!" Raskolnikov smiled awkwardly, making every effort to look him straight in the face, but failing. He suddenly added:
"I only say that because I suppose there were a great many pledges, and it must be hard to remember them all. Yet you remember them all so clearly, and—"
"Stupid! Feeble!" he thought. "Why did I add that?"
"But we know everyone who had pledges, and you're the only one who hasn't come forward," Porfiry answered with barely perceptible irony.
"I haven't been quite well."
"I heard that too. I heard you were in considerable distress. You still look pale."

"I'm not pale at all! No, I'm perfectly well," Raskolnikov snapped rudely and angrily, completely changing his tone. Anger was rising in him and he couldn't hold it back. "And in my anger I'll give myself away," flashed through his mind. "Why are they tormenting me?"

"Not quite well!" Razumihin jumped in. "What next! He was unconscious and delirious all yesterday. Would you believe, Porfiry—as soon as our backs were turned, he got dressed, though he could barely stand, gave us the slip, and went off on some escapade until midnight, delirious the whole time! Can you imagine?"
"Really delirious? You don't say!" Porfiry shook his head in a womanish way.
"Nonsense! Don't believe it! But you don't believe it anyway," Raskolnikov let slip in his anger. But Porfiry Petrovitch didn't seem to catch those reckless words.

"How could you have gone out if you weren't delirious?" Razumihin flared up. "What did you go out for? What was the point? And why on the sly? Were you in your right mind? Now that the danger's passed, I can speak plainly."

"I was sick of them yesterday," Raskolnikov addressed Porfiry suddenly, with a smile of insolent defiance. "I ran away to rent a room where they wouldn't find me, and took a lot of money with me. Mr. Zametov there saw it. Tell me, Mr. Zametov—was I in my right mind yesterday, or delirious? Settle our dispute."
He could have strangled Zametov at that moment, so hateful were his expression and his silence.
"In my opinion, you spoke sensibly and even cleverly, but you were extremely irritable," Zametov said drily.
"And Nikodim Fomitch was telling me today," Porfiry Petrovitch put in, "that he ran into you very late last night at the lodging of a man who'd been run over."

"And there," Razumihin said, "weren't you out of your mind? You gave your last penny to the widow for the funeral. If you wanted to help, give fifteen or twenty, but keep at least three roubles for yourself. Instead you threw away the whole twenty-five!"

"Maybe I found a treasure somewhere that you don't know about. That's why I was so generous yesterday. Mr. Zametov knows I've found a treasure! Forgive us for taking up your time with such trivialities," he said to Porfiry with trembling lips. "We must be boring you."
"Oh no, quite the contrary! If you only knew how much you interest me! It's fascinating to watch and listen. And I'm really glad you've come forward at last."
"How about some tea? My throat's parched," Razumihin cried.
"Excellent idea! Perhaps we'll all join you. Wouldn't you like something stronger before tea?"
"Get out of here!"
Porfiry Petrovitch went out to order tea.
Raskolnikov's thoughts were in turmoil. He was in terrible agitation.

"The worst of it is they don't even bother to disguise it! They don't stand on ceremony! How did you come to discuss me with Nikodim Fomitch if you didn't even know me? They don't care to hide that they're tracking me like a pack of hounds. They simply spit in my face." He was shaking with rage. "Come on then, strike openly—don't play with me like a cat with a mouse. That's hardly polite, Porfiry Petrovitch, and perhaps I won't stand for it! I'll stand up and throw the truth in all your faces, and you'll see how I despise you." He could barely breathe. "But what if it's all in my imagination? What if I'm wrong and just getting angry out of inexperience, not keeping up my wretched act? Maybe it's all unintentional. All the usual phrases, but there's something about them. It could all be said innocently, but there's something. Why did he say 'with her' so bluntly? Why did Zametov add that I spoke 'cleverly'? Why that tone? Yes, the tone. Razumihin is sitting right here—why doesn't he see anything? That innocent blockhead never sees anything! Feverish again! Did Porfiry just wink at me? Of course not—nonsense! Why would he wink? Are they trying to rattle me, or teasing me? Either it's all in my head or they know! Even Zametov is rude. Is Zametov rude? He's changed his mind. I predicted he would. He's at home here; it's my first visit. Porfiry doesn't treat him like a guest—sits with his back to him. They're thick as thieves, no doubt conspiring against me! They were surely talking about me before we came. Do they know about the apartment? If only they'd get on with it! When I said I ran off to rent a flat, he let it pass. I slipped that in cleverly—might be useful later. 'Delirious,' indeed! Ha-ha-ha! He knows all about last night! He didn't know my mother had arrived! The old woman had written the date in pencil! You're wrong—you won't catch me! There are no facts, only guesswork! Show me the facts! Even the flat isn't a fact but delirium. I know what to tell them. Do they know about the flat? I won't leave without finding out. What did I come for? But my anger right now—that might be a fact! Fool, how irritable I am! Maybe that's the right approach—play the sick man. He's probing me. He'll try to trip me up. Why did I come?"
All this flashed through his mind like lightning.
Porfiry Petrovitch returned quickly. He suddenly became more jovial.
"Your party yesterday, brother, has left my head a bit foggy. And I'm out of sorts altogether," he began in a completely different tone, laughing to Razumihin.
"Was it interesting? I left you at the most interesting point. Who won the argument?"
"Oh, nobody, of course. They got onto the eternal questions and floated off into the clouds."
"Just imagine, Rodya, what we got into yesterday. Whether crime really exists. I told you we talked ourselves hoarse."
"What's strange about that? It's an ordinary social question," Raskolnikov answered indifferently.
"The question wasn't framed quite like that," Porfiry observed.

"Not quite, that's true," Razumihin agreed at once, getting heated and hurried as usual. "Listen, Rodion, and tell us your opinion. I want to hear it. I was fighting tooth and nail and wanted your help. I told them you were coming. It started with the socialist doctrine. You know their position: crime is a protest against the abnormality of the social order and nothing more—no other causes are admitted!"
"You're wrong there," cried Porfiry Petrovitch, noticeably animated and laughing as he looked at Razumihin, which made him even more excited.
"Nothing else is admitted!" Razumihin interrupted heatedly.

"I'm not wrong! I'll show you their pamphlets. Everything with them is 'the influence of environment' and nothing else. Their favourite phrase! From which it follows that if society is properly organized, all crime will vanish at once, because there'll be nothing to protest against and everyone will become righteous in an instant. Human nature isn't taken into account—it's excluded, it's not supposed to exist! They don't accept that humanity, developing through a living historical process, will eventually become a normal society. They believe a social system designed by some mathematician's brain will instantly organize all of humanity and make it just and sinless, faster than any living process! That's why they instinctively hate history—'nothing but ugliness and stupidity in it'—and they explain everything as stupidity! That's why they so despise the living process of life. They don't want a living soul! The living soul demands life; it won't obey the rules of mechanics; it's suspicious, it's reactionary! But what they want, even though it smells of death and can be made of rubber, at least isn't alive, has no will, is servile and won't rebel! And in the end it all comes down to building walls and planning rooms and corridors in a commune! The commune is ready, but human nature isn't ready for it—it wants life, it hasn't completed its vital process, it's too early for the graveyard! You can't leap over nature with logic. Logic admits three possibilities, but there are millions! Cut away a million and reduce everything to the question of comfort! That's the easiest solution! Seductively clear—and you don't even have to think! That's the main thing—you mustn't think! The whole secret of life in two pages of print!"

"Now he's off—beating the drum! Grab hold of him!" Porfiry laughed. "Can you imagine," he turned to Raskolnikov, "six people going on like that last night, in one room, with punch to warm things up! No, brother, you're wrong. Environment accounts for a great deal in crime, I can assure you."
"Oh, I know it does. But just tell me this: a man of forty violates a ten-year-old child. Was it environment that drove him to it?"
"Well, strictly speaking, it was," Porfiry observed with noteworthy gravity. "A crime of that nature might well be attributed to the influence of environment."

Razumihin was nearly beside himself. "Oh, if you like," he roared, "I'll prove to you that your white eyelashes can be attributed to the fact that the Ivan the Great bell tower is two hundred and fifty feet tall! I'll prove it clearly, precisely, progressively, and even with a liberal slant! Care to bet?"
"Done! Let's hear how he'll prove it!"

"He's always bluffing, damn him!" cried Razumihin, jumping up and gesticulating. "What's the use of talking to you? He does it all on purpose. You don't know him, Rodion! He took their side yesterday just to make fools of them. And the things he said! And they were thrilled! He can keep it up for two weeks straight. Last year he convinced us he was entering a monastery—he stuck to it for two months. Not long ago he announced he was getting married and had everything ready for the wedding. He even ordered new clothes. We all started congratulating him. There was no bride, nothing—pure fantasy!"
"Wrong! I got the clothes first. It was the new clothes that gave me the idea of fooling you."
"Are you that good a dissembler?" Raskolnikov asked carelessly.

"You'd never have guessed, would you? Just wait—I'll fool you too. Ha-ha-ha! No, I'll tell you the truth. All these questions about crime, environment, children remind me of an article of yours that interested me at the time. 'On Crime,' or something like that—I forget the exact title. I read it with pleasure two months ago in the Periodical Review."
"My article? In the Periodical Review?" Raskolnikov asked in astonishment. "I did write an article about a book six months ago, when I left the university, but I sent it to the Weekly Review."
"But it appeared in the Periodical."
"And the Weekly Review folded, so that's why it wasn't published at the time."
"That's right. But when it folded, the Weekly Review was absorbed into the Periodical, and so your article appeared two months ago. Didn't you know?"
Raskolnikov had not known.
"Why, you could get paid for it! What a strange person you are! You lead such a solitary life that you don't know about things that concern you directly. It's a fact, I assure you."

"Bravo, Rodya! I didn't know either!" cried Razumihin. "I'll run to the reading room today and ask for that issue. Two months ago? What was the date? Doesn't matter—I'll find it. Imagine not telling us!"
"How did you find out the article was mine? It's only signed with an initial."
"I learned quite by chance, the other day, through the editor. I know him. I was very much interested."
"As I recall, I analyzed the psychology of a criminal before and after the crime."

"Yes, and you argued that committing a crime is always accompanied by illness. Very, very original—but that wasn't the part that interested me most. It was an idea at the end of the article that, I'm sorry to say, you only hinted at without fully developing. There's a suggestion that certain people can—not exactly that they're able to, but that they have a perfect right to commit crimes and break moral laws, and that the law doesn't apply to them."
Raskolnikov smiled at the exaggerated and deliberate distortion of his idea.
"What? A right to commit crime? But not because of environmental influence?" Razumihin asked with some alarm.

"No, not exactly," Porfiry answered. "In his article, all people are divided into 'ordinary' and 'extraordinary.' Ordinary people must live in submission and have no right to break the law, because they're ordinary. But extraordinary people have the right to commit any crime and transgress any law, simply because they're extraordinary. That was your idea, if I'm not mistaken?"
"What? That can't be right," Razumihin muttered in bewilderment.
Raskolnikov smiled again. He saw the point at once and knew where they were trying to drive him. He decided to accept the challenge.

"That wasn't quite my argument," he began simply and modestly. "Still, I admit you've stated it almost correctly—perhaps perfectly so." He almost enjoyed admitting this. "The only difference is that I don't claim extraordinary people are always obliged to commit crimes, as you put it. I doubt such an argument could even be published. I simply suggested that an 'extraordinary' person has the right—not an official right but an inner right—to decide in his own conscience to overstep certain obstacles, and only when it's essential for the practical fulfillment of his idea, which may sometimes benefit all of humanity. You say my article is unclear; I'm prepared to make it as clear as I can. Perhaps I'm right in thinking you want me to—very well. I maintain that if the discoveries of Kepler and Newton could not have been made known without sacrificing the lives of one, a dozen, a hundred, or more people, Newton would have had the right—would indeed have been duty-bound—to eliminate that dozen or hundred for the sake of making his discoveries known to all humanity. But it doesn't follow that Newton had a right to murder people randomly or steal at the market every day. Then, I recall, I argue in my article that all legislators and leaders of men—Lycurgus, Solon, Mohammed, Napoleon, and so on—were without exception criminals, since in establishing new laws they violated old ones handed down from their ancestors and held sacred by the people, and they didn't shrink from bloodshed either, if that bloodshed—often of innocent people bravely defending the old ways—served their cause. It's remarkable, in fact, that the majority of these benefactors and leaders of humanity were guilty of terrible carnage. In short, I maintain that all great men, or even those slightly out of the ordinary—anyone capable of saying something new—must by their very nature be criminals, to a greater or lesser degree. Otherwise they can't break out of the common rut, and to remain in it is something they can't accept, again by their very nature, and in my view they shouldn't accept it. You see there's nothing particularly new in all that. The same thing has been printed and read a thousand times before. As for my division of people into ordinary and extraordinary, I admit it's somewhat arbitrary, but I don't insist on exact numbers. I only believe in my central idea: that by a law of nature, people are generally divided into two categories. The first—the inferior, the ordinary—is material that serves only to reproduce its kind. The second category consists of people who have the gift or talent to say a new word. There are, of course, countless subdivisions, but the distinguishing features of both categories are fairly clear. The first category—generally speaking, people conservative by temperament and law-abiding—live in obedience and love being obedient. As I see it, it's their duty to be obedient, because that's their calling and there's nothing humiliating in it. The second category all transgress the law; they are destroyers, or inclined to destruction, according to their abilities. The crimes of these people are of course relative and varied. Most often they seek, in very different ways, the destruction of the present for the sake of something better. But if such a person must, for the sake of his idea, step over a corpse or wade through blood, he can, I maintain, find within himself, in his conscience, a justification for doing so—depending on the idea and its scope, note that. It's only in that sense that I speak of their right to crime in my article—you'll recall it begins with the legal question. There's no need for alarm, though. The masses will almost never grant this right; they punish and hang such people, more or less, thereby quite justly fulfilling their conservative calling. But those same masses, in the next generation, put these criminals on a pedestal and worship them, more or less. The first category is always the person of the present; the second, the person of the future. The first preserves the world and multiplies it; the second moves the world and leads it to its goal. Both have an equal right to exist. In short, for me everyone has equal rights—and vive la guerre éternelle—until the New Jerusalem, of course!"
"Then you do believe in the New Jerusalem?"
"I do," Raskolnikov answered firmly. As he said this, and throughout his entire preceding speech, he kept his eyes fixed on one spot on the carpet.
"And do you believe in God? Forgive my curiosity."
"I do," Raskolnikov repeated, raising his eyes to Porfiry.
"And do you believe in the raising of Lazarus?"
"I do. Why do you ask all this?"
"You believe it literally?"
"Literally."
"I see. I asked out of curiosity. Forgive me. But let's return to the question. They aren't always executed. Some, on the contrary—"
"Triumph in their lifetime? Oh yes, some achieve their ends in this life, and then—"
"They begin executing others?"
"If necessary. In fact, for the most part they do. Your observation is quite witty."

"Thank you. But tell me this: how do you distinguish these extraordinary people from the ordinary ones? Are there signs at birth? I feel there ought to be more precision, some external markers. Forgive the natural concern of a practical, law-abiding citizen, but couldn't they adopt a special uniform, for instance? Wear something distinctive, be branded in some way? Because, you see, if confusion arises and a member of one category imagines he belongs to the other and begins 'eliminating obstacles,' as you so aptly put it, then—"
"Oh, that happens quite often! That remark is wittier than the last."
"Thank you."

"Don't mention it. But note that the mistake can only arise in the first category, among the ordinary people, as I perhaps unfortunately called them. Despite their predisposition to obedience, a great many of them, through some quirk of nature sometimes granted even to a cow, like to imagine themselves advanced thinkers, 'destroyers,' and to push their way into the 'new movement'—quite sincerely, too. Meanwhile, the truly new people are often unnoticed or even scorned as reactionaries. But I don't think there's much danger here. They never go very far. Of course they might get a thrashing now and then to teach them their place, but nothing more. In fact, even that's hardly necessary, since they punish themselves—they're extremely conscientious. Some perform this service for each other, others do it to themselves with their own hands. They'll impose various public acts of penance on themselves, with beautiful and edifying results. In short, you have nothing to worry about. It's a law of nature."

"Well, you've certainly set my mind at rest on that score. But here's another concern. Tell me, please: are there many people who have the right to kill others—these extraordinary people? I'm prepared to bow before them, of course, but you must admit it's alarming if there are a great many of them."

"Oh, you needn't worry about that either," Raskolnikov went on in the same tone. "People with new ideas, people with even the faintest capacity for saying something new, are extraordinarily rare. One thing is clear: the emergence of all these grades and subdivisions must follow some law of nature with unfailing regularity. That law is unknown at present, but I'm convinced it exists and may one day be discovered. The vast mass of humanity is merely raw material, existing only so that by some great effort, some mysterious process, some crossing of races and bloodlines, the world might at last produce one person in a thousand with a spark of independence. Perhaps one in ten thousand is born with still greater independence, one in a hundred thousand with more still. The man of genius is one in millions, and the great geniuses—the crown of humanity—appear perhaps one in many thousand millions. In short, I haven't peered into the crucible where all this takes place. But there certainly is, and must be, a definite law. It can't be a matter of chance."
"Are you two joking?" Razumihin cried at last. "Sitting there making fun of each other? Are you serious, Rodya?"

Raskolnikov raised his pale, almost sorrowful face and gave no reply. The unconcealed, persistent, nervous, and discourteous sarcasm of Porfiry seemed strange to Razumihin set against that quiet, mournful face.

"Well, brother, if you're really serious—you're right, of course, that the idea itself isn't new, that it's like what we've read and heard a thousand times. But what is truly original in all this, what is exclusively your own—and horrifies me—is that you sanction bloodshed in the name of conscience, and, forgive me, with such fanaticism. That, I take it, is the main point of your article. But this sanctioning of bloodshed by conscience is, to my mind, more terrible than the official, legal sanctioning of it."
"You're quite right—it is more terrible," Porfiry agreed.
"Yes, you must have exaggerated! There's some mistake. I'll read it. You can't think that! I'll read it."
"None of that is actually in the article. There's only a hint of it," said Raskolnikov.

"Yes, yes." Porfiry couldn't sit still. "Your attitude toward crime is fairly clear to me now, but forgive my impertinence—I'm truly ashamed to keep bothering you—but there are certain practical possibilities that trouble me. What if some man or youth imagines himself a Lycurgus or a Mohammed—a future one, naturally—and decides to remove all obstacles? He has some grand enterprise before him and needs money for it, and so he tries to get it. Do you see what I mean?"
Zametov gave a sudden guffaw from his corner. Raskolnikov didn't even glance at him.
"I must admit," he went on calmly, "that such cases certainly do arise. The vain and foolish are particularly prone to falling into that trap—young people especially."
"You see? Well, then what?"

"What then?" Raskolnikov smiled. "That's not my fault. It happens and always will. He just said"—he nodded at Razumihin—"that I sanction bloodshed. Society is well enough protected by prisons, exile, investigators, and hard labor. There's no need to worry. You have only to catch the thief."
"And what if we do catch him?"
"Then he gets what he deserves."
"You're certainly logical. But what about his conscience?"
"Why should that concern you?"
"Simple humanity."
"If he has a conscience, he'll suffer for his mistake. That will be his punishment—on top of prison."
"But the real geniuses," Razumihin asked, frowning, "those who have the right to murder? Shouldn't they suffer at all, even for the blood they've shed?"

"Why the word 'should'? It's not a question of permission or prohibition. He will suffer if he's sorry for his victim. Pain and suffering are always inevitable for a great intelligence and a deep heart. The truly great must, I think, experience great sorrow on earth," he added dreamily, no longer in the tone of the conversation.
He raised his eyes, looked at them all thoughtfully, smiled, and picked up his cap. He was too calm compared to how he'd entered, and he felt it. Everyone stood up.

"Well, you can abuse me, be angry with me if you like," Porfiry Petrovitch began again, "but I can't resist. Allow me one more little question—just one small idea I want to express so I don't forget it."
"Very well, tell me your little idea," Raskolnikov stood waiting, pale and grave.

"Well, you see, I really don't know how to put it properly. It's a playful, psychological thought. When you were writing your article, surely you couldn't have helped fancying yourself—just a little—an 'extraordinary' man, someone uttering a new word, in your sense of the term. Isn't that so?"
"Quite possibly," Raskolnikov answered contemptuously.
Razumihin stirred.
"And if so, could you bring yourself—in case of hardship or in service to humanity—to overstep those obstacles? For instance, to rob and murder?"
And again he winked with his left eye and laughed noiselessly, just as before.
"If I did, I certainly wouldn't tell you," Raskolnikov answered with defiant, haughty contempt.
"No, I only asked for the literary interest, in connection with your article."
"How blatant and insulting!" Raskolnikov thought with revulsion.
"Allow me to point out," he answered drily, "that I don't consider myself a Mohammed or a Napoleon, or any figure of that kind, and since I'm not one of them, I can't tell you how I would act."
"Oh come—don't we all think ourselves Napoleons in Russia these days?" Porfiry Petrovitch said with alarming familiarity.
Something peculiar betrayed itself in his very tone of voice.
"Perhaps it was one of these future Napoleons who did for Alyona Ivanovna last week?" Zametov blurted out from the corner.

Raskolnikov said nothing but looked firmly and intently at Porfiry. Razumihin was scowling darkly. He had already begun to notice something. He looked angrily around. A minute of grim silence passed. Raskolnikov turned to leave.

"Going already?" Porfiry said amiably, extending his hand with excessive courtesy. "Very, very glad to have met you. As for your request, have no concerns—write to me as I described, or better yet, come to my office in a day or two—tomorrow, even. I'll be there at eleven, certainly. We'll arrange everything, have a talk. As one of the last people to have been there, you might be able to tell us something," he added with the most good-natured expression.
"You want to question me officially, in proper form?" Raskolnikov asked sharply.

"Why? That's not necessary for now. You misunderstand me. I just never miss an opportunity, and I've spoken with everyone who had pledges. I've taken statements from some of them, and you're the last. Yes, by the way," he cried, as if suddenly struck by a thought, "I just remembered something!" He turned to Razumihin. "You were going on to me about that Nikolay fellow. Of course I know, I know perfectly well," he turned to Raskolnikov, "that he's innocent, but what can one do? We had to bother Dmitri too. Here's the thing: when you went up the stairs that day, it was past seven, wasn't it?"
"Yes," Raskolnikov answered, with the unpleasant feeling that he needn't have said it.

"And when you went up between seven and eight, did you happen to see, on the second floor, in an open apartment—two workmen, or at least one? They were painting in there. Did you notice them? It's very, very important for them."

"Painters? No, I didn't see them," Raskolnikov answered slowly, as though searching his memory, while in reality he was straining every nerve, nearly fainting with anxiety to figure out where the trap lay. "No, I didn't see them, and I don't think I noticed any open apartment on that floor. But on the fourth floor," he said, having now mastered the trap and feeling triumphant, "I remember someone was moving out of the flat across from Alyona Ivanovna's. Some porters were carrying out a sofa and they squeezed me against the wall. But painters—no, I don't recall any painters, and I don't think there was any apartment open. No, there wasn't."
"What do you mean?" Razumihin suddenly shouted, as though something had clicked. "The painters were there on the day of the murder, and he was there three days before! What are you asking about?"

"Ah, I've mixed it up!" Porfiry slapped his forehead. "Damn this case—it's turning my brain!" He addressed Raskolnikov almost apologetically. "It would mean so much to us to find out whether anyone saw them between seven and eight in that apartment. I thought perhaps you could tell us something. I completely mixed up the dates."
"Then you should be more careful," Razumihin remarked grimly.
These last words were spoken in the hallway. Porfiry Petrovitch saw them to the door with excessive politeness.
They walked out into the street, gloomy and silent, and for several steps neither said a word. Raskolnikov drew a deep breath.
